item.title: IDEA: Octa Fleece vs Polartec Alpha Direct FAQ
item.description:
Source: Sectionhiker.com
Octa Fleece and Polartec Alpha Direct are both ultralight, highly breathable synthetic insulations, but they achieve this through different fabric constructions. Octa generally provides a smoother, more abrasion-resistant outer face, while Alpha Direct maximizes airflow, low weight, compressibility, and drying speed at the expense of durability. Octa is made from a specialized hollow polyester fiber with eight radial projections, giving the yarn a gear- or octopus-like cross-section. The hollow center and projecting “fins” create insulating air spaces while using less polymer than a conventional solid yarn. In finished fabric, Octa is commonly made as a two-sided construction: - A relatively smooth, tighter-knit or mesh-like outer face. - A brushed, raised inner face containing the lofted Octa fibers. - A stable knit or mesh base that anchors the insulation. - Open spaces within the structure that reduce weight, increase airflow, and help limit water retention. Some Octa fabrics use a grid or diamond-like knit, while others resemble a conventional fleece with a flat outer surface and fuzzy interior. The main design advantage is that the insulating pile is protected on the inside, while the outer face resists snagging, abrasion, and wind. This makes Octa more practical as a standalone midlayer than very open fleece fabrics, although it is still not windproof and generally benefits from a wind shell in exposed conditions. Alpha Direct is a low-density, open fleece structure designed to function without a separate backing or lining fabric. It consists of loosely arranged polyester fibers and fleece tufts held in a light lattice-like structure; in lighter versions, the fabric may be partly transparent. Its construction is characterized by: - No conventional protective face fabric. - Open, lofty fiber tufts that trap air. - Very high air permeability. - Minimal material between the wearer and the insulation. - Low mass, high compressibility, and rapid drying. The absence of a face fabric is central to Alpha Direct’s performance. It removes weight and lets moisture vapor and body heat escape easily, but it also exposes the fuzzy structure to snagging, abrasion, pilling, and tearing. Octa feels more like a conventional technical fleece. Its inner pile provides warmth and softness, while the smoother exterior slides more easily under a shell and is less likely to catch on vegetation. The denser outer structure also slightly reduces convective heat loss, so it can feel warmer in cool, calm conditions without an extra wind layer. Alpha Direct feels more like wearing a breathable insulation web. It is particularly effective during stop-and-go activity because it provides insulation without trapping as much excess heat as traditional fleece. During sustained exertion, its open structure lets sweat vapor and heat escape quickly. The difference becomes most noticeable in wind. Octa’s face fabric offers some protection, while Alpha Direct lets wind pass through readily. A lightweight windshirt can turn Alpha Direct into a highly efficient system: the shell blocks convective heat loss while keeping the fleece light and breathable. Without that shell, Alpha Direct works best in sheltered conditions or during high-output activity. Which is better? - Choose Octa when durability, standalone use, moderate wind resistance, and a smoother outer surface matter most. - Choose Alpha Direct when you prioritize minimum weight, maximum breathability, fastest drying, and superior performance under a windshirt or rain shell. - For bushwhacking, scrambling, or frequent wear without an outer layer, Octa is the safer choice. - For ultralight backpacking, high-output hiking, trail running, or variable-intensity activity, Alpha Direct usually offers the highest performance-to-weight ratio, provided it is protected from abrasion. In short, Octa is a more protected, versatile fleece construction, while Alpha Direct is a more open, specialized insulation construction. Octa sacrifices a small amount of breathability for durability and wind resistance; Alpha Direct sacrifices protection for exceptional airflow, low weight, and fast drying. SectionHiker never accepts payment for gear reviews or editorial coverage. When you buy through affiliate links on our site, we may earn a small commission at no extra cost to you. Help us continue to test and write unsponsored and independent gear reviews, hiking and backpacking FAQs, and free hiking guides.

item.title: INSTRUCTION: How to get upgraded to first class by using overbooked flights to your advantage
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
Moving to the front of the plane is a dream for most economy passengers. But many don’t know where to start when working out how to get upgraded to first class. Sure, there are a few ways to be certain that you’ll be considered for an upgrade, like having gold status with the airline or simply opting to cash in points and miles to secure a more premium seat. But if you aren’t loyal to one airline and you don’t have miles to speak of, are there other ways to get a free upgrade? Here are our top tips to scoring a free flight upgrade on your next trip. One strategy that sparks debate among frequent flyers is trying to negotiate an upgrade when a flight is overbooked. Airlines often maximise profits by selling more tickets than there are seats on planes, in anticipation that some passengers will miss the flight or change their plans at the last minute. When all passengers show up at the gate – or when airlines need to fly crew to another airport on a sold-out plane – gate agents need volunteers to give up their seats and get bumped to a later flight. It’s a situation that has happened more often since the pandemic – and one that you could potentially capitalise on. Gate agents want to avoid bumping passengers against their will, so they’re authorised to offer incentives like travel vouchers, gift cards and other perks. Some frequent flyers say it’s possible to request an upgrade to first class as part of giving up your seat. But the negotiation takes a lot of finesse – if a gate agent will entertain it at all. “This has happened, but as a general matter doesn’t work often,” says Gary Leff, an aviation expert who writes the blog View From the Wing. Usually, gate agents prefer to sweeten the deal by increasing the amounts of travel vouchers or gift cards instead, according to Leff. However, just because requesting an upgrade instead of a voucher is a little unorthodox, it doesn’t mean it’s off the table. “In situations where they’re really motivated to get volunteers, [requesting an upgrade] might work, but another snag is that there need to be premium seats available on alternate flights,” Leff says. “Increasingly, premium cabins are full in advance and there aren’t leftovers to do this with.” Do your research and check other flight availability That means that if you do want to negotiate an upgrade request as a condition of being bumped, doing your research will be key. Look at the next few flights on the airline’s website and see what seats are available. Identify which flight you’d ideally like to be upgraded on. Then approach the gate agent and kindly state your request. The best case for a free upgrade a traveller could make to a gate agent would be if no economy seats are available on the next flight but premium seats are open, according to Brett Snyder, president of Cranky Concierge, a firm that offers air travel assistance. “A traveller can say, ‘If you can get me on that next flight, I can go,’” Snyder says. Confirm your upgrade before giving up your seat Spelling out the specific details of your offer is important. “You should state clearly what you want when offering to volunteer,” Leff advises. Because a gate agent will have to sign off on any upgrades, it’s not possible to make such a request online and must go through the representative at the gate desk, according to Leff. After you make your request, the gate agent will likely need to look into it and further assess what’s possible. Remember, they’re juggling a lot of details, all under strict time constraints. Try to sit close to the gate desk to monitor the situation but don’t hover or be bothersome. If the gate agent agrees to a first class upgrade, be sure to re-confirm the change has been processed before they move you to the later flight. “An overworked gate agent might add you to the volunteer list, not really internalising the specifics of what you’ve asked for,” Leff says. “Don’t assume they’re delivering on what you said your requirements were. Make sure you are certain you have it before giving up your seat.” Remember that while it’s certainly possible, getting upgraded is not considered the standard compensation by most airlines for oversold flights. So pick the right situation and be respectful and patient with gate agents. “Airlines have tried to make oversold flights as uncomplicated as possible for agents,” Snyder says. “They don't really have the time or interest in trying to negotiate side deals in most cases.” Getting upgraded in this manner is certainly not a straightforward process, but that doesn’t mean it’s not worth giving it a shot. “A traveller can always try,” Snyder says. “There's no harm in asking.” This story originally featured on cntraveler.com

item.title: Alaska Airlines plans unique Anchorage-Tokyo service — with a single-aisle plane — in 4-route expansion
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
Alaska Airlines plans unique Anchorage-Tokyo service — with a single-aisle plane — in 4-route expansion Alaska Airlines executives were not kidding when they said more growth in Asia was coming. The Oneworld alliance carrier just announced its newest service to Tokyo, which will start next spring. But unlike the airline's other transpacific routes, this one will not launch from Seattle — and it will not be on one of its large twin-aisle planes. Beginning in May 2027, Alaska plans to connect its hub at Ted Stevens Anchorage International Airport (ANC) to Tokyo's Narita International Airport (NRT). The new route, Alaska's first-ever nonstop flight to Japan from its namesake state, is part of a larger four-route expansion at ANC, unveiled Tuesday. The expansion also includes a trio of new domestic routes to Texas and Tennessee. The four new Alaska routes are: - ANC - NRT: Daily from May 13, 2027, through Sept. 7, 2027; resuming three-times weekly in January 2028 - ANC - Austin Bergstrom International Airport (AUS): Saturdays from June 12, 2027, through Aug. 7, 2027 - ANC - Dallas Fort Worth International Airport (DFW): Saturdays from June 12, 2027, through Aug. 7, 2027 - ANC - Nashville International Airport (BNA): Saturdays from June 12, 2027, through Aug. 7, 2027 All four of those routes will be flown with Alaska's Boeing 737 MAX 8 — yes, that includes the service to Tokyo. The aircraft features 16 domestic first-class seats, 36 extra-legroom and 115 standard economy seats. The Anchorage-Tokyo service will build on Alaska's existing service from Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA) to NRT, which launched in 2025. But with this route operated by a narrow-body MAX 8, there will be no true long-haul business-class product up front — just the domestic first-class recliners. Japan is a key focus for Alaska's expansion in Asia. Tokyo was Alaska's first long-haul destination from Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA) last year. And, on top of this new nonstop from Anchorage, the carrier recently announced nonstop service from SEA to Osaka's Kansai International Airport (KIX), also beginning next May. Hawaiian and Alaska merged in 2024, and this growth builds on Hawaiian Airlines' strength in Japan. Hawaiian continues to fly to KIX and Tokyo's Haneda Airport (HND) from its Honolulu hub. Further growth in Japan could be coming: Alaska intends to join the immunized joint venture with American Airlines and JAL, which, if approved by regulators, would allow it to coordinate commercial activities between the U.S. and Japan with the other two airlines. Alaska will be the first airline to fly the MAX 8 to NRT from North America with its new nonstop from ANC. The route will stretch 3,433 miles and take around eight hours of flying time. That may sound like a long trek for the narrow-body, domestic-configured aircraft, However, this new ANC-NRT route does not even rank among the 10 longest MAX 8 routes globally, according to schedule data from aviation analytics firm Cirium. Even Alaska's own nonstop from Seattle to Keflavik International Airport (KEF) in Iceland is longer, at 3,622 miles. "The [MAX] 8 is so good at going long distances for us. [Anchorage] will see a lot of that," Shane Tackett, Alaska's president and chief financial officer, said at an investor event in September. Alaska faces little competition on its new routes from ANC. Its partner American Airlines flies between ANC and DFW, while AUS and BNA are both currently unserved, according to Cirium schedules. The ANC-NRT route is also unserved today. But the route holds a unique place in aviation history: It was once a key leg on flights to Japan before the advent of long-range aircraft. Air France, British Airways, JAL, KLM Royal Dutch Airlines and SAS Scandinavian Airlines all flew the route as part of a refueling stop at ANC into the early 1990s, Cirium schedules show. The arrival of the Boeing 747-400 in 1989 enabled many airlines, including U.S. carriers Northwest Airlines and United Airlines, to drop ANC as a fuel stop in favor of nonstop flights to Japan. item.title: IDEA: 6 Places in the US Where Travelers Can Hunt, Fish, or Forage for Their Own Food
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
My boyhood summers tasted like wild fruit and fish. When I gathered blueberries from the pine and oak woods around my father’s New Hampshire home, he would stir their purple sweetness into pancake batter. When I pulled brook trout from the waters of a long-abandoned granite quarry, I would sauté them in a cast iron skillet until delicate flesh flaked from translucent bone. At twenty, I went vegan and quit fishing. For food, I looked to the grocery store and, seasonally, the garden. Though I still gathered the occasional handful of berries or chanterelles, I took little sustenance directly from wild nature. Ten years later—my black-and-white dietary ethics shaken by the realities of agriculture and my body demanding a wider array of nutrients—I began a journey back to omnivory and the wild. I took up a fishing rod again. I paid more attention to mushrooms emerging from the forest floor. And I began learning to hunt. Picking portobello-like indigo milk caps, casting for trout or striped bass, or sitting at the base of a maple with rifle in hand as dawn brightened the frosty deer woods, I began to remember that the land is a source not only of beauty but also of food, that the earth feeds our bodies as well as our souls. Over the past two decades, I have gradually awakened to this continent’s vast diversity of wild edibles and to the deep meanings wild foodways still carry across cultures. Many of us, of course, have lost these practices. We have forgotten how to eat wild. If you want to reconnect with the entire nature-to-plate experience, you need to get out there and harvest with your own hands. Even if you aren’t ready to dive into relearning ancient skills, across the country you can find opportunities to experience wild foods, each a gift flavored by local land and culture, each a chance to savor what a place tastes like, straight from the source. Foraging the forests of Asheville, North Carolina People have walked the Blue Ridge Mountains in search of edibles since the end of the last Ice Age. Of the tens of thousands of species that inhabit the region’s lush and astonishingly biodiverse forests today, a handful dominate Asheville’s vibrant foraging and culinary scene. Ramps, or wild leeks, bring the earthy, garlicky promise of spring. Pawpaws, the continent’s largest edible native fruit, ripen in late summer and early fall, delivering a near-tropical blend of mango and banana to the tongue. And a bounty of edible fungi—from morels and black trumpets to lion’s mane, chanterelles, and chicken of the woods—fill mushroom hunters’ baskets in every season but winter. Overharvesting, both legal and illegal, has triggered some restrictions. In Great Smoky Mountains National Park, for example, the collection of ramps has been forbidden since 2004 and daily mushroom harvest is limited to a pound per person. The prohibition on gathering ramps extends to the Eastern Band of Cherokee, though a recent agreement with the National Park Service permits several dozen members to gather sochan within park boundaries. Outside the park, opportunities still abound for all. In the nearby Pisgah and Nantahala National Forests, for instance, you can gather up to three pounds (or one gallon) of ramps or mushrooms for personal use, though truffles and chaga are off limits. Even if you don’t see yourself setting off into the woods in search of dinner, or exploring foraging possibilities within Asheville itself, the area offers a cornucopia of ways to enjoy and learn about wild edibles. - No Taste Like Home offers foraging tours, including a forage-to-table program that lets you bring wild ingredients to local restaurants, where chefs prepare them for you. - The Market Place restaurant, a James Beard Award semi-finalist in 2025, often serves locally foraged mushrooms. - At Asheville Farmers Markets, vendors offer pawpaws and other wild foods in season. - The Rainbows and Ramps festival, hosted by the Eastern Band of Cherokee in late March, includes a meal featuring local ramps and rainbow trout. - The early May Waynesville Ramp Convention features a ramp dinner and Appalachian music and dancing. Swap blue crab for blue catfish in Chesapeake Bay Covering nearly 4,500 square miles, the Chesapeake Bay and its tidal tributaries are famous for blue crabs, beloved by locals and visitors alike. Though the bay still supplies a significant portion of the nation’s catch, blue crab numbers have been impacted by habitat loss, overharvest, and predation. Among the crab’s predators are locally invasive blue catfish. Introduced to Virginia rivers decades ago, the fish have proved able to tolerate the saltier waters of the bay and are now outcompeting native species. To mitigate the negative impacts, diverse stakeholders—including scientists, government agencies, seafood producers, restaurants, and grocery stores—are working to build a thriving “River to Table” market. In recent years, Virginia and Maryland have each recorded millions of pounds in annual commercial blue catfish harvest. Though consumers are advised to eat smaller fish or to trim away belly fat and dark meat to remove contaminants, blue catfish is increasingly popular table fare. Delicious fried, grilled, smoked, or blackened, it is available in a growing number of restaurants and grocery stores around the region. You can also catch your own, with or without a fishing guide. In most tidal waters, neither state limits how many blue catfish recreational anglers can keep. If you go, be prepared for some big, hard-fighting fish. Blue cats regularly run 30-plus pounds and can get much larger. - From Skrimp Shack fast food to the elegance of Dauphine’s, many local restaurants serve blue catfish. - Maryland’s Best maintains a catfish-focused directory of restaurants and grocery stores, including Wegmans, Safeway, and Whole Foods. - Among many other local fishing guides, Capital Blues Fishing and Goober Time can help you catch your own. - Depending on where you want to fish, a non-resident fishing license from D.C., Virginia, or Maryland lets you head out on your own for the day, week, or year. - The Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum gives visitors the chance to learn about the history of the bay, including its storied bounty of wild foods. Centuries ago, the Anishinaabe migrated from the Atlantic coast to the western Great Lakes region. At the heart of their migration stories is a prophecy telling them to travel west until they found the place where food grows on water. That food was manoomin, or wild rice, an annual grass that grows in shallow water. An important traditional food for multiple Indigenous nations, wild rice (psiŋ in Dakota) continues to carry deep cultural meaning and is central to food sovereignty efforts in the western Great Lakes region. To harvest wild rice in late summer, two people work from a canoe, one navigating with a long forked pole, the other using a pair of smooth cedar sticks to gently bend tall stalks over the gunwales and tap the ripe grain loose. (Mechanized harvest has been banned in Minnesota since 1939.) Knowledge of when and how to harvest is passed down by other harvesters and comes with experience. Once dried and parched, grain must be separated from chaff. Though some people still use traditional methods, most finishing is now done mechanically. Nutty and smoky, manoomin works any time of day, from rice and berries with maple syrup for breakfast to a hearty stew for dinner. Natural wild rice grains are a mix of earthy hues and cook in 20 minutes or less. In contrast, “paddy” or “cultivated” variants grown in Minnesota and California are glossy black and take much longer. Minnesota law requires clear labeling to distinguish the two. Though Minnesota residents and nonresidents alike can purchase a wild rice license, harvesting and processing is a complex process. For Tribal communities, it is also an ancient and ongoing relationship. For those new to ricing, learning from experienced harvesters or attending a Tribal-led camp or educational event is a respectful place to begin. Visitors can also support Tribal communities by purchasing manoomin directly from them. - The Minnesota Department of Natural Resources posts harvest outlooks and maps on its wild rice management page. Generally, state-managed waters are open to public harvest, while federally- and tribally-managed waters are not. - Indígena by Owamni in Minneapolis serves manoomin, among many other wild and cultivated foods native to the Americas. - Autumn Harvest Ojibwe Wild Rice sells wood-fire-parched rice at the St. Paul Farmers’ Market. - Native Harvest, part of the White Earth Land Recovery Project, sells wild rice online. - Festivals, camps, events, and workshops organized by Tribal nations, intertribal organizations, and municipalities offer opportunities to learn about (and eat) wild rice, especially in September. Dubbed the “Gloucester of the Gulf,” the commercial fishing hub of Pensacola, Florida, anchored a late 19th- and early 20th-century fishery that hauled in millions of pounds of red snapper each year. After World War II, recreational fishing surged as well. The pressure, combined with bycatch from shrimp trawlers, proved too much: between 1950 and 1990, red snapper numbers plunged. Since the 1990s, federal managers have capped the annual catch, split it between commercial and recreational fishermen, and limited anglers to two fish per day. Sweet, mild, and firm, red snapper can be roasted as Snapper Veracruzana, fried as snapper bites, baked whole with Thai seasonings, or grilled with lemon sauce. You’ll find it at seafood markets along the Florida panhandle and Alabama coast. You’ll also find it at restaurants, many of which will cook your catch. Snapper season peaks in summer but often runs into fall. Many snapper are released because they’re undersized, out of season, or over the two-fish limit. When anglers reel up a snapper from deep water, the fish’s swim bladder often expands, leaving it unable to swim back down. To keep released fish alive, Florida Sea Grant’s Return ’Em Right program urges anglers to use descending devices, which return fish quickly to depth, and offers free devices to those who complete an online course. In recent years, federal rules have also required anglers to carry them. - Joe Patti's Seafood, a Pensacola waterfront market since 1930, sells red snapper fillets and other Gulf seafood. - Numerous local guide services, including Panhandle Charters, Pelican Adventures, and O Sea D Fishing Charters, offer snapper-focused fishing trips. - Many restaurants in Destin, Pensacola, and Orange Beach will cook your cleaned catch, and some, like Harbor Docks, combine fishing trips with restaurant preparation. - Each October, the Destin Fishing Rodeo offers a month-long fishing tournament experience for anglers of all ages. In the 1860s, the British colony of Hong Kong gave the Kingdom of Hawaiʻi eight axis deer. The beautiful spotted animals, native to India, were released on the island of Molokaʻi. In the absence of predators, they multiplied swiftly. In 1959 and 1960, nine deer were relocated to Maui. There, too, numbers soared. Alongside other large herbivores, none of which are native to Hawaiʻi, axis deer have devastated crops and stripped hillsides of drought-stressed vegetation, allowing rain to erode soil and sweep it into wetlands and onto coral reefs, harming critical habitats. To accelerate deer control measures, Hawaiʻi has issued more than two dozen emergency proclamations in recent years. Many families hunt deer and prize the meat, especially on Molokaʻi, but hunting alone hasn’t kept numbers in check. So islanders have turned to an unconventional solution: commercial harvest. State and federal laws ban nearly all sale of wild game in the US, but federal rules allow USDA inspection and then sale of some non-native species, including axis deer. In 2007, Molokaʻi hunter Desmund Manaba became the first in Hawaiʻi to win approval to harvest axis deer and sell the meat. In 2012, Maui County backed a harvesting cooperative of its own. Today, shooters working for Maui Nui Venison take deer from private ranches each night. Fresh or processed into snack sticks, most of the meat is sold. A portion is distributed for free to local families through the company’s Holo ʻAi program, which the company links to Hawaiʻi’s long tradition of food-sharing and which helped ensure food security during the COVID-19 pandemic and after the devastating 2023 wildfires. - If you’d like to cook your own, you can buy Maui Nui Venison online and in local stores. - With a nonresident license and hunter education from Hawaiʻi or another state, you can hunt in a public game management area. - You can also hunt with a professional outfitter, such as Pu‘u O Hōkū Ranch on Molokaʻi, which offers conservation-focused hunts as well as cabins and a lodge. Gather the fruits of the desert in Tucson, Arizona The word “desert” may conjure ideas of emptiness, barrenness, a lack of life. Sitting on the eastern edge of the Sonoran Desert, Tucson, Arizona, dispels all such notions. Designated as a UNESCO Creative City of Gastronomy in 2015, Tucson boasts both the longest continuous agricultural history of any city in the United States and a rich set of wild foods traditions. Among other plants, cacti are on the menu. For millennia, Tohono O’odham people have gathered food from—and maintained vital relationships with—multiple species, following a calendar set by the desert’s two rainy seasons. From late summer into fall, during and after the summer rains, people harvest prickly pear fruit, which can be eaten raw or squeezed into juice. In spring, after the winter rains, harvesters pluck cholla buds. Reminiscent of lemony asparagus tips, they can be cooked and eaten fresh or dried for later use. In June, before the summer rains return, people gather saguaro fruit, knocking it from towering cacti with a kuipad, a long pole made of saguaro ribs, then dry the protein-rich seeds and make jam from the fruit. They also make syrup, fermenting some into wine for the rain ceremony that marks the O’odham New Year. Foraging is prohibited in Saguaro National Park, with exceptions for O’odham harvesting traditions. Though gathering is legal on private land with permission, participating in guided harvests and walks is an ideal place to begin. You can also purchase foods gathered by O’odham harvesters. - San Xavier Co-op Farm, run by members of the Tohono O’odham Nation, sells wild foods, including cholla buds and mesquite flour. - Mission Garden hosts public events and classes and grows heritage crops on an O’odham site that has been under cultivation for 4,000 years. - The Tohono Chul Sonoran Botanic Garden offers guided walks from September through May and the Arizona-Sonora Desert Museum offers a guided saguaro fruit harvest each June. - Sonoran House Sam Hughes, Barrio Bread, and Ursa use local ingredients, including prickly pear and mesquite. - The Tucson Meet Yourself festival, held each October, features many local food vendors.

item.title: IDEA: Cycling in the wild heart of the Netherlands: an autumnal break in the Veluwe
item.description:
Source: The Guardian Travel
One minute I’m cycling through an expansive dusty pink stretch of heathland with sloping sand dunes in the distant horizon, the next I’m winding through a fragrant Scots pine forest as sunlight filters through the branches of red-barked trees to make a kaleidoscope of white shapes on the trail floor ahead. I’m in Hoge Veluwe National Park, a 5,400 hectare (13,000 acre) nature reserve in Gelderland, about an hour and a half from Amsterdam. It’s crisscrossed by 25 miles (40km) of cycling paths, and around 2,000 free-to-use white bikes are available for visitors to explore the ever-changing scenery. I’ve been flitting back and forth to the Netherlands for years and have lost count of the times friends there have raved about the park and the wider Veluwe region, a forest-rich ridge of hills and diverse landscapes, stretching 37 miles, north to south. Finally I’ve come to see for myself and explore on foot and on two wheels over a few days – adding in a dash of culture at some of its historic towns and museums too. My trip starts at Natuurcentrum De Ginkel, a charming nature and visitor centre near Ede outside Arnhem. Here I meet nature guide Hanna Pol who takes me into the forest. “Veluwe is very biodiverse,” says Pol quietly as we walk past verdant oak, pine and birch. Trees with autumnal tawny-coloured leaves line one side of the path and wildflowers, with pops of bright yellow sunflowers and vivid red poppies, the other. Pol reels off some of the wildlife here: roe deer, five types of woodpecker, beavers, wild boar and wolves. As we crunch through a carpet of fallen leaves, we spy a small brown frog on a log, a woodpecker dancing around a tree, and the outline of two rust-red deers in the distance. We make our way to the wildlife observation area, an enclosed building with curved windows and a theatre-style set of wooden chairs. “The deer pass this way every night to eat,” says Pol. “Once we saw a really big fight break out.” She’s seen wolves too – they returned to the country in 2015 after about 150 years and it’s a controversial topic, with farmers worried about their livestock. We don’t see the elusive creatures, just a solitary bright white buzzard perching on a tree. On the shelves behind us, an assortment of skeletal remains includes antlers, skulls, the teeth of a wild boar and the foot of a deer. That night I stay in a stylish and sleek cabin with floor-to-ceiling views of the forest at Buitenplaats Petersburg on the edge of the park. It’s a peaceful haven of lodges with fairy lights strung around the woods and an enchanting Italian restaurant, Il Lupo, with an outdoor terrace. Besides its unspoilt natural wonders, Veluwe has plenty of other attractions. I visit Paleis Het Loo, a 17th-century royal palace in Apeldoorn, once the summer residence and hunting lodge of William of Orange III and his wife Princess Mary II Stuart. It’s an impressive building with ornate rooms, a staircase with the second biggest mural in the Netherlands, formal symmetrical gardens and an underground museum which tells the story of the Dutch royal family. Hotel de Echoput, a family-run modern hotel nearby, surrounded by the forest, is my home for the night. Its Grand Bistro Echo is a treat, with a menu that focuses on local ingredients – I enjoy fried mushrooms with a creamy Dordogne sauce and a vegan cheesecake with basil and white chocolate. The next morning, after a brisk walk in the woods with barely a soul around, I visit the historic Hanseactic city of Harderwijk, on the shores of Wolderwijd lake. I wander the narrow cobblestone streets, medieval city walls and Old Town Hall with guide Marianne van Limbeek. “Harderwijk means hiding place for shepherds,” she tells me. We bump into Hendrik Kaper, a local street organist wearing a flat cap who treats us to a rendition of Bohemian Rhapsody on his portable wooden organ. But it’s in Hoge Veluwe national park that I find the greatest sense of serenity – though one day a small adder with a dark zigzag stripe stops me in my tracks. Come outside peak times, as I have, and you might have some of the trails to yourself. Within the park lies Kröller-Müller Museum, a revered national art museum and sculpture garden founded by art collector Helene Kröller-Müller, who along with her husband, shipping magnate Anton Kröller, bought vast amounts of land in Veluwe (their private estate was later donated to the state). My timing is great as all 88 of its Vincent van Gogh paintings are on show together for the first time since 1984 (until 3 January).
The sculpture park is one of the largest in Europe, and I stroll around the surrounding open grass and into the forest and stumble across various artworks (there are about 200 pieces dotted around). A short cycle away is Jachthuis Sint Hubertus, the former country residence of the Kröller-Müller family with a watchtower more than 30m tall (apparently Helene loved afternoon tea at such lofty heights) surrounded by a lake with a very athletic bunch of jumping carp. I stop at Restaurant De Hoge Veluwe at Park Paviljoen for an early pasta dinner on the terrace before the sky turns a moody grey and rain looks imminent. Fortunately it’s only a 15-minute cycle to Otterlo, a pretty village with clusters of fairy lights and bunting decorating red brick houses and Vakantieoord Het Lorkenbos, a charming holiday park surrounded by trees. My bungalow is cute and, feeling as if I’m in a twinkling winter wonderland, I light a candle and look up the Dutch word for cosy. It’s gezellig – a perfect description of how I feel after my nourishing break in this wild and restorative part of the Netherlands. The trip was arranged by Visit Veluwe. Entrance to Hoge Veluwe national park €13.85 per adult. Cabins at Buitenplaats Petersburg from €110. Camping at Het Lorkenbos from €23 a night, bungalows from €320 for two nights. Double rooms at De Echoput from €169. Omio provided train travel: Eurostar runs from London to Amsterdam

item.title: IDEA: Why You Might Find Yourself Fishing, Foraging—Or Even Hunting—On Your Next Vacation
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
There are two types of luxury hotels these days: Those where you don’t have to lift a finger. And those where you might find yourself elbow-deep in the cavity of an elk that you, of all people, just harvested. As in: stalked, shot, and gutted, and butchered. Camouflage not your style? Maybe you’re digging chanterelles in windswept western Scotland. Or prying mussels off rocks along South Africa’s Cape Peninsula. Or: totani-fishing off the Amalfi Coast in a wooden boat built by a local fisherman whose family has been squid fishing in the Tyrrhennian Sea for generations. (And then, yes, cleaning it, cooking it, and eating the totani e patate of your dreams.) Whatever you’re doing, if you’re a food-obsessed traveler in 2027, you may find yourself foraging, fishing, or even hunting on your next trip. Call it the next iteration of farm-to-table—but one thing is clear: The hospitality industry has officially gone wild. At some of the world’s most exclusive hotels, old-world service is giving way to old-world skills. The kind most urban-dwelling, laptop-pecking, Door Dash-ordering professionals have lost. And are looking to gain... on vacation. “Travelers are increasingly curious about the culture behind what they eat,” says Leopoldo Elefante, executive chef at Casa Angelina, on the cliffs of Praiaono, Italy, which launched its “totani ritual” last year, and other local culinary experiences like it. (Nighttime ancient lantern fishing or Pomodoro picking, anyone?) Whether it's couples, kids, or grandparents, it appears that everyone wants to get their hands dirty. “They don’t simply want to taste a local dish, they want to understand where the ingredients come from.” In other words: people don’t just want to enjoy an exceptional supper anymore, they want to help source it. It begs the question (and a butchered metaphor): Why are people paying to milk a cow when they can get, say, a bowl of fresh yogurt with housemade granola, local berries, and drizzled with maple syrup for $26? For Clare Sammells, an associate professor of anthropology who focuses on food and tourism at Bucknell University, the answer lies in the liberating nature of travel. “Travel allows you to try things you’d never do in your daily life,” she explains. “You’re in a new, sacred space. You don’t have to set an alarm and put on a suit and go to an office. You can eat and drink whatever you like! Suddenly doing something outside your normal life starts to seem more possible. Maybe you can envision yourself as someone who does butcher a hog.” It’s not that big of a leap from the farmers’ market, really. Sampling persimmons from a guy growing six varieties in California’s Central Valley. Picking huckleberries around Montana. Diving for sea snails in South Africa. It all stems from the same, ever-deepening desire: to know where our food comes from. This is not a new craving, of course. We lazy food-lovers have been trying to find our way back-to-the-land ever since factory farming and the industrial meat complex destroyed it. And, we keep getting closer! We’ve strolled all the local organic markets, and thanked the farmers on all the menus. We’ve attended all the fancy dinners in all the fields and toured all the chef’s gardens. Now we want to don gumboots and tromp through the woods and pull up our own porcinis! Wrangle into wetsuits and snorkel off the craggy coast of Sonoma and collect a dozen different seaweeds! Trod gently over tide pools and pluck purple sea urchin and slurp super fresh uni! We want to get … closer. Personal. Not just to our food but, well, to the earth itself. We want to, you know, touch grass. And then eat it. (Wheat, bristle, bent, all fair game.) And inns, influencers, outfitters, and chefs from Santa Barbara to Sussex are making it possible, perfecting the art of what could be called five-star self-sufficiency. Take Vermejo, Ted Turner Reserve’s 558,000-acre wildlife reserve in New Mexico, once a traditional hardcore hunting lodge. Today, it offers bison safaris, snowtubing, and spa treatments– as well as hunting and fishing trips catering to those who want a cushy bed with their cow elk or cutthroat trout—and a talented chef to either teach them how to filet it, prepare it, and pair it. Plus a conservationist who can explain the role hunting plays in biodiversity and conservation. This idea may be a novel trend for some travelers, but for Indigenous communities across North America, sustainable hunting, fishing, and foraging has always been a fundamental part of daily life. Today, adventurous travelers can respectfully connect with that ancient knowledge by staying at Indigenous-owned lodges like Wahous Wilderness Lodge, the Ahousaht First Nation’s flagship hospitality venture in British Columbia’s remote Clayoquot Sound (which offers fishing experiences and a “tide-to-table” culinary philosophy), or by dining at Indigenous- focused restaurants helping revitalize Native American foodways from Oaxaca to Minneapolis. Hotels and restaurants aren’t the only ones getting the claytonia perfoliata-curious out there. Independent foraging guides are multiplying like mushrooms after a rain. From niche Instagrammers like @feminist_fisherwoman to YouTube stalwarts like @catchncookcalifornia and Taku Kondo (@outdoorcheflife), they are making the outdoors our oyster—leading such hands-on adventures as crab snaring in Half Moon Bay, spearfishing in Santa Barbara, and quail hunting in Tucson. That’s what happens when people get a taste of eons-old traditions—and berries beyond the grocery store—says Nick Weston, founder of Hunt Gather Cook: They hunger for more. He has been bringing “newbies” from London to Los Angeles to Shepherd’s Barn on his Firle Estate, in Sussex, since 2011. His butchering courses and live-fire feasts sell out. “The only thing I’ve found people are uncomfortable with is cutting off a rabbit’s head with a machete.” Understandable. Not all wild food requires far-flung travel, nor a steel stomach. Alexis Nikole Nelson–aka @blackforager—instructs her almost three million followers on how to eat acorns. Her first cookbook, brilliantly titled “Happy Snacking, Don’t Die!” is already being devoured by the masses, along with her recipes for Pine Shortbread Cookies and Milkweed Buds. Whether you’re going nuts in your own backyard or spearfishing lionfish off the coast of Florida, connecting with your environment in this way “sparks a true sense of place that can develop into a deeper sense of environmental stewardship,” says Sam Shepherd, a biology professor and director of agriculture and catholic environmental stewardship at Ava Maria University in the Scottish Highlands. Today, such slow immersion in a local food system is increasingly accessible to travelers, Shepherd explains, adding that it "contrasts starkly with tourism based on brief curated visits in which the local food and culture can become a side-show.” On the North Fork of Long Island, Lin Beach House takes a more laidback approach. Run by the married duo behind Matchbook Distillery, Brian Kwasnieski, a commercial fisherman, and his wife, Leslie Merinoff Kwasnieski, the contemporary six-room Victorian invites people to, per the website: “Pull the fish. Cut the herbs. Blend the gin. Come back for dinner.” And people do. Pickling, clamming, and preserving, too. “We’ve had a lot of financial analysts lately,” says Leslie with a laugh. “People love scooping the fish!” Brian practices the sustainable method of pound trap fishing, which avoids bycatch, she explains. He usually heads out on his boat at 4 a.m. to bring in pufferfish, porgy, and mackerel. Wait, guests get up at 4.am.? “Oh, no,” Leslie corrects. “We let them sleep in until 10.” It is vacation after all.

item.title: INSTRUCTION: Cornbread Dressing With Sausage
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit
This is not your typical Southern cornbread dressing recipe (or cornbread stuffing, if you prefer). Sure, it has plenty of melted butter, onions, celery, and sage-rich breakfast sausage. And yes, the top bakes up golden and crisp, while the interior stays tender and almost but not quite custardy. But in our Making Perfect: Thanksgiving series, Rick Martinez and Chris Morocco gave the Thanksgiving staple a wake-up call via hot chiles and something perhaps even more unexpected: corn nuts. But don’t worry about hard little nuggets in your dressing; we’re after the flavor, not the crunch. Pulverized into a fine powder and bloomed in butter with the aromatics, the corn nuts bring an earthy sweetness and seriously amp up the corn flavor. You can use store-bought cornbread or a box mix, but we developed our Buttermilk Cornbread recipe specifically with stuffing in mind. Whichever you choose, drying the cubes in the oven helps them hold their shape as they soak up the stock. If the liquid pools when you first add it, let the cornbread absorb it for a few minutes before transferring everything to the baking dish. What kind of cornbread is best for dressing? A sturdy cornbread that holds its shape when soaked with stock is ideal. Molly Baz’s buttermilk cornbread recipe was developed specifically for making stuffing, but store-bought cornbread works too. Just don’t skip the oven-drying step, which helps keep the dressing from turning mushy. Are there any substitutes for the corn nuts? If you can’t find corn nuts, try finely ground Fritos, which have a similar earthy flavor, or another plain corn chip. Several readers have reported good results with this swap. You can also leave the corn nuts out altogether, though you’ll lose some of the concentrated corn flavor that makes this dressing distinctive. Can I make this cornbread dressing without sausage? Yep! But you’ll need to make a few other adjustments. If going for a totally vegetarian stuffing, you can easily swap in vegetable stock, but since the sausage provides a host of savory flavor, you’ll need to compensate. Add 1–2 Tbsp. soy sauce or a pinch of MSG in with the wine. You can also double up on the dried herbs—especially the sage—since breakfast sausage brings in those flavors as well. Watch Rick and Chris make cornbread dressing Need to make a substitution? - Step 1Preheat oven to 325°. Divide 1 batch Buttermilk Cornbread or 3 lb. store-bought cornbread, cut into pieces (14–16 cups ¾" cubes) evenly between 2 large rimmed baking sheets and bake, tossing occasionally, until dried out and lightly browned around the edges, 40–50 minutes. Let cool at least 10 minutes. Increase oven temperature to 350°. Step 2Meanwhile, cook 1½ lb. breakfast sausage, casings removed if needed, in a large skillet over medium-high heat, stirring and breaking up with a spoon, until lightly browned and cooked through, 6–8 minutes. Transfer to a plate. Step 3Reduce burner to medium heat and melt 1 cup unsalted butter (2 sticks) in same skillet. Add 2 medium onions, chopped, and 4 celery stalks, chopped; season with kosher salt. Cook, stirring occasionally, until softened but not browned, 8–10 minutes. Add 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and 2 Thai chiles or 1 jalapeño (with seeds), chopped. Cook, stirring once, until very fragrant, about 1 minute. Add ¾ cup corn nuts, finely ground in a food processor, blender, or mortar and pestle (about ½ cup) and cook, stirring often, until very fragrant and vegetables are starting to brown around the edges, about 3 minutes. Add ¾ cup dry white wine and cook, stirring occasionally, until almost completely evaporated, about 3 minutes. Add 1 Tbsp. finely chopped sage and 2 tsp. finely chopped thyme and toss to combine. Remove from heat. Step 4Combine cornbread, sausage, and sautéed vegetable mixture in a large bowl. Whisk 3 large eggs and 3½ cups turkey stock or low-sodium chicken broth in a medium bowl until very well combined. Pour over cornbread mixture and let sit, gently stirring every minute or so, until cornbread has absorbed all or virtually all of the liquid. Season with kosher salt (about 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal or 1½ tsp. Morton kosher salt) and freshly ground black pepper. Step 5Lightly butter a 3-qt. or 13x9x2" casserole dish. Transfer stuffing to dish and tap dish lightly against counter to distribute and compact stuffing. Cover tightly with aluminum foil and bake until stuffing is very hot throughout and bubbles appear around sides, 40–45 minutes. Increase oven temperature to 425° and remove foil. Continue to bake stuffing until top is lightly browned, 15–20 minutes longer. Do ahead: Stuffing can be baked at 350° 3 days ahead. Let cool, then chill. Reheat in a 350° oven before increasing temperature to 425° and removing foil. Editor’s note: We first published this cornbread dressing recipe in October 2019 as “Cornbread Stuffing With Sausage and Corn Nuts” as part of our Absolutely, Positively Perfect Thanksgiving Menu. Head this way more of our favorite Thanksgiving sides →

item.title: Where was the new Harry Potter series filmed? The quintessentially British locations used to bring the magic to life (again)
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
On Location peels back the curtain on some of your favourite films, television shows, and more. This time, we ask: where was HBO's Harry Potter filmed? Ever since the first Harry Potter film adaptation hit cinemas back in 2001, fans of the franchise have made special pilgrimages to visit the locations seen on screen – from Glenfinnan Viaduct to Alnwick Castle. For many, it is a tangible way of experiencing the magical wizarding world of their imaginations, allowing them to step inside the places that have become so closely associated with Harry, Ron, Hermione et al. This Christmas, a new generation will be introduced to Harry Potter and the gang via an ambitious television adaptation, with a series planned for each book. As well as introducing us to the next roster of up-and-coming stars, it will no doubt put new filming destinations on the map too, adding to the long list of places where we can experience the wonder of the Hogwarts universe up close. And while the majority of the series has been filmed at Warner Bros. Studios Leavesden, there have been mysterious reports of road closures and sightings of actors with wands around the country. Of course, we can’t know for certain which settings will stand in for which places in the fictional wizarding universe – but we can say that you should consider adding these locations to add to your next Harry Potter-related road trip itinerary… Where was the new HBO Harry Potter series filmed? In late September, the Buckinghamshire village of Latimer was taken back to the 1990s for three days when filming took place for the second series of the show. The village green was transformed into a traditional fete, with period-appropriate cars seen lining it. With 17th- and 18th-century cottages neighbouring the area, it’s got that quintessentially English countryside charm, so it’s no wonder it was used. It’s unclear which part of the book that will be set here, though it could be something to do with Harry visiting the Weasleys at their home before school starts. Last October, residents of Skipton, a market town in North Yorkshire, were surprised to see an actor wielding a wand standing on a rooftop on a normal suburban street. The filming took place on Westmoreland Street, under the code name ‘Apollo’, but it’s pretty clear what was happening. With terraced Victorian houses, it’s a typical English street that could be standing in for just about anywhere in the Harry Potter universe. Locals were especially excited – though this is far from their first filming rodeo. House of Guinness was also filmed in the picturesque town, which is dubbed ‘the gateway to the Yorkshire dales’, in 2024. Lustleigh in Devon stands in for Godric’s Hollow, the village where Harry Potter was born and where his parents were killed. Featuring Grade II-listed 15th-century thatched granite cottages and winding medieval lanes, it’s easy to see why it was chosen. Indeed, if you close your eyes and imagine the perfect historic English village, this would be it – they even have an annual May Day festival where the ‘May Queen’ is crowned. It’s a great place for outdoorsy types to visit too, with incredible walking and cycling paths in the surrounding Lustleigh Cleave woods.Kynanc Kynance Cove and Cadgwith Cove, Cornwall John Lithgow, our new Dumbledore, and Dominic McLaughlin, our new Harry Potter, have been spotted filming various scenes on Cornwall’s dramatic coastline. The mythic Kynance Cove served as the backdrop to a meeting shot between Dumbledore and the Flamels (the owners of the philosopher’s stone of the first book's title), while the charming fisherman’s village of Cadgwith Cove was used for a scene involving Harry and the Dursleys. You can easily visit both in a day, as they are located on the Lizard Peninsula. The leafy Hertfordshire town of Hoddesdon will be the fictional Surrey town of Little Whinging in the new series, the place where Harry grows up with his aunt, uncle and cousin, the Dursleys. The actor who plays Uncle Vernon, Daniel Rigby, has been spotted filming scenes, reportedly bumping into a purple-cloaked wizard in the scene. Located just 45 minutes outside of London, residents were reportedly delighted it had been chosen. McLaughlin and Nick Frost (who plays Hagrid) were both seen in costume filming in Borough High Street in August 2025. With its cobblestones, winding market stalls and railway arches, we reckon it could be a great option for when Hagrid takes Harry shopping in Diagon Alley. Interestingly, nearby Stoney Street was used for the exterior of the Leaky Cauldron when the original films were made, so it could even be that Borough High Street is standing in for that. Other filming in London has reportedly taken place at Embankment and London Zoo.

item.title: REVIEW: Carl Friedrik’s aluminium check-in suitcase review: Is this the last suitcase you will ever need to buy?
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
Carl Friedrik launched its aluminium cabin case back in March of this year but, until recently, if you wanted a full set of the Succession-approved suitcases, you’d be limited to its Core and Hybrid ranges. Which, to be honest, is no bad thing – several of our editors have known, loved and used these cases for years and years; they’re some of the slickest-looking luggage on the market, with a lifetime warranty to match. Nonetheless, for frequent travellers especially, there’s something lovely about owning a full suitcase set, and now the brand has released a full aluminium check-in suitcase to accompany your shining carry-on. It was a good move. An aluminium suitcase is an undeniably lovely thing. They’re made from the exact same material as an aircraft, which makes it feel uniquely well-placed to handle the rigours of the hold, while harking back to an exciting Golden Age of Travel when everyone seemed just that little bit more stylish. Plus, it’s undeniable that wheeling a glimmering suitcase around the terminal makes your long haul schlep feel more elevated – it makes you feel more put together when you’re about to embark on a tedious endeavour in your less-than-glamorous loungewear in a tiny economy seat. That’s exactly what you’ll get here. The case is finished in Carl Friedrik's signature streamlined ridged design, with twin TSA-approved combination locks – banishing the inevitable busted zips forever – and smart Italian leather details. It’s luggage clearly crafted for travellers who demand a strong aesthetic alongside robust security. But, costing £795, it’s also an investment purchase. Does its real-world performance match its premium price tag? To give it a thorough test, I took the new Carl Friedrik aluminium check-in on a week-long journey across Vietnam – putting its capacity, lock mechanism and overall durability to the test through two long-haul flights, one overnight train, and a six-hour coach journey. Here’s how it held up under pressure. Pros and cons of the Carl Friedrik’s Aluminium Check-in case at-a-glance Pros: - Exceptional build quality and Italian leather accents - Perfectly proportioned for a week-long trip without feeling cumbersome - Remarkably scuff-resistant exterior that holds up well against airport handling - Smooth, whisper-quiet spinner wheels for effortless gliding across terminals Cons: - Aluminium shell is weightier than polycarbonate alternatives - Heavy-duty clasps can prove tricky to close when the case is packed to capacity - Rigid frame offers zero exterior give or stretch for last-minute extras Surely the biggest draw. Sheeny aluminium looks special to behold and, from the moment you lift the handle, this case exudes quiet luxury. It swaps standard zippers in favour of a reinforced aluminium frame sealed by two heavy-duty latch locks, with vegetable-tanned Italian leather detailing on the handles and body, which adds a warm, tactile contrast against the cool metallic finish. Remember that aluminium suitcases are notoriously prone to dings and scratches. Most people consider this part of the charm; a tale of a life well travelled. Nonetheless, at such a price point, I did wince a little at the thought of my sparkly new case emerging at Hanoi airport with noticeable scuffs (if this is really intolerable to you, see our guide to the best suitcase covers). Remarkably, despite a 12-hour-plus journey in the cargo to Vietnam, it emerged virtually unblemished – coming off the carousel with nary a scratch. I was genuinely surprised – this marks a major plus-point for the material for me. By the time it had come on and off the train, the coach, and the return flight home, it had only a few tiny hairline scratches, none that were visible without real scrutiny. Inside, the case offers a clean, open layout designed to maximise usable packing volume across both main compartments. It has a removable compression pad on one side, plus a zipped mesh pocket on the other. For a seven-day itinerary, the 76L capacity hit the sweet spot – accommodating a week’s worth of layers, footwear, my washbag and travel accessories. The compression straps pull tight to keep contents anchored during transit, and they do a good job. Take note: your packing mileage may vary. If you’re headed off to the beach for two weeks, it may be perfect to use for a caseful of slinky dresses and bikinis. If you’re packing for a longer trip, a winter getaway, or for more outdoorsy endeavours, you may have to pack light, or look elsewhere. I ambitiously packed in some walking boots, a spare raincoat and jumper for hiking in the mountains, and had to sit on it to get it closed after squeezing in a few souvenirs on location. At one point, I resigned myself to the fact that I might not get it shut at all. I did in the end, but it was a struggle. Bear this in mind if you’re gearing up for a two-week getaway – or really like to shop. The case performs beautifully on the move, thanks to Japanese Hinomoto 360-degree spinner wheels, which deliver a near-silent, effortless glide across smooth airport concourses and bumpy street pavements alike. The multi-stage telescopic handle locks securely into place without annoying wobble, and it didn’t get sticky lifting it up and down even when full-to-bursting, which isn’t something I can say about all suitcases I’ve tested. My only friction point was the aforementioned mild issue getting it closed when the case is very full, when getting the dual locking clasps lined up and snapped shut took some effort. However, it’s very satisfying when it snaps shut, and feels far more secure than a zip – you’ll simply never have an issue with it bursting open mid-flight. For me, that peace of mind is worth the minor strain to get a very full case shut. When the case is not heaving, there’s no issue with the clasps whatsoever. The Carl Friedrik Aluminium Check-in case is a beautifully crafted piece of luggage that balances sophisticated aesthetics with resilience. It’s a beautiful, hardwearing and overtly high-quality piece, and a solid investment for frequent flyers looking to elevate their luggage game. It is a little heavier than the brand's polycarbonate alternative, and £250 more expensive. If the allure of the aluminium is less pressing for you, the editor-tested Hybrid Check-In is an excellent alternative. Regardless, if you're happy to make an investment, this case has a lifetime warranty, so you can be confident that this the last money you’ll need to spend on your case ever – and it will always look lovely, on each and every outing. Key specs: - Matching items? Yes, an aluminium carry-on More editor tried-and-tested Carl Friedrik suitcases For further recommendations, explore our other guides:

item.title: As Rivers Swamped New Mexico, Raft Guides Paddled Through Flooded Streets to Rescue Stranded Pets
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine
Desert River Guides co-founder Cody Dudgeon stands holding a dog with another rescue volunteer (Photo: Courtesy of Ryan Dudgeon) Ryan Dudgeon emerged from waist-deep quicksand, her raspberry-pink drysuit caked in desert mud. The Farmington, New Mexico, whitewater paddler towed a 14-foot inflatable raft through flooded streets with a team of fellow guides on October 23. The group was searching for pets left behind after historic flooding devastated the Four Corners region the night before, destroying homes and displacing thousands. Using their swiftwater rescue skills and drysuits, Ryan and her volunteer team spent several days rescuing animals stranded in flooded homes, locked in corrals, or trapped in submerged kennels and cages. “We are the only ones in the county qualified to do anything like this, aside from Search and Rescue,” Ryan, 41, told Outside over the phone. Ryan and her husband Cody, 46, own Desert River Guides, a rafting company that leads trips down the Animas and San Juan Rivers. The couple has lived in Farmington their entire lives and said they have never experienced flooding like this. “We aren’t used to natural disasters here,” Ryan said. “None of us know what to do because we’ve never dealt with something like this.” With guidance from the Farmington Regional Animal Shelter and the City of Farmington, the Dudgeons turned their commercial rafting warehouse and equipment into a temporary emergency animal shelter and holding area for lost pets after the floods. “We have kittens and puppies all over the place,” Ryan said. “More and more are showing up now that the waters have receded and other people are finding lost animals.” Across the Four Corners region, community members have been displaced and their homes decimated; rockslides have closed trails like Bridal Veil Falls in Utah, and Lake Powell has risen at least ten feet since the flooding began. Ryan believes their guide shop will store animals—chickens, cats, dogs, rabbits, and more—for weeks to come. Over the phone, Ryan described the heartbreak of on October 23. She knew she had to do something to help her community. “We got in our dry suits, loaded up the van with the boat, and we went out there,” Ryan said. The group paddled their raft through inundated neighborhoods and, where possible, walked the streets while towing it. “People needed help,” she said. “People were scared. They left their homes, but they also left their pets locked inside their houses, which is why we went out.” The Dudgeons rescued dozens of animals, pets, and livestock that were left behind. Farmington is an agricultural community with thousands of ranches and farms in the surrounding San Juan County. Ryan recalled trying to reach a goat farm and hearing the animals bleating in the distance. The team of paddlers was unable to reach the goats and, like many other livestock, the herd drowned. “There were dead animals everywhere,” Ryan said. “People were calling us, and we went out with our boats and gear, and we spent two days trying to rescue animals in rafts and float people out. Just as much as we could help, just as much as we were allowed to do.” Deceased pigs, horses and goats floated through the streets alongside housing debris and logjams. “I heard them drowning,” Ryan said. Longtime residents like the Dudgeons compared the event to the historic 100-year floods of October 1911, when historic rains tore through the Four Corners region. The 2026 floods have been so bad that, Ryan said, rumors circulated through town that a nearby dam had broken. In reality, it was just flooding from swollen rivers. Rivers are measured in cubic feet per second (CFS). One cubic foot is roughly the size of a basketball. The Animas River, for example, usually runs between 1,000 and 4,000 CFS, but on October 26 it was pushing 12,000 CFS—roughly that many basketballs pummeling through one point every second. The Dudgeons usually raft the nearby San Juan River at around 500 CFS. During peak floods, it surged to 33,500 CFS in Farmington. Many residents have lost everything. A friend is staying with her now after the floodwaters inundated his house, she said. Now it’s filled with nearly one foot of mud. “He can’t go home, and he doesn’t know what to do,” Ryan said. “He has nowhere else to go.” Upstream, mobile home parks in Bloomfield and areas downriver through Shiprock and the Navajo Nation suffered severe inundation, with homes washed off foundations and submerged to the rooflines. “Trailers were moved off the foundations and houses were taken downstream—they’re stuck on bridges or on the side of the river,” Ryan said. “They’ve lost everything. I can’t imagine how long this recon will take. It’s literally unbelievable.” Floodwaters also left behind thick layers of contaminated river mud that make re-entering inundated homes nearly impossible, Ryan said. Sewage treatment plants have been flooded, further contaminating waterways in the area. “None of us know what to do because we’ve never dealt with something like this,” Ryan said. Shortly after the Dudgeons opened their warehouse to the animals, officials placed the shop under an immediate flood watch around 10 P.M. on October 23. “We moved out all of our rafts onto the bus, and started moving animal crates in,” Ryan said. “And then all of a sudden, after we got everything perfectly set up, officials called us around 10 P.M. on a Friday night.” Her friends and colleagues called and showed up to help move the animals and their things out of the building to another on higher ground. “It was just the most incredible community involvement, and I will never be able to thank these people enough,” Ryan said. “It was just the most incredible community involvement, and I will never be able to thank these people enough.” The following morning, she said up to four inches of rain fell within ten minutes, flooding the town. “I have my whole life in that building,” Ryan said. “Rain was just pouring down the hills, all toward our shop and river. The river was breaching its banks.” For now, the warehouse houses not only rescued animals but also those keeping them safe. People stay at the warehouse, sleeping on the guide company’s camping gear, using the pool table and grill, and cooking breakfast on the camp stoves. “It’s a rafting company, and now it’s a rafting company turned into an animal shelter,” Ryan said. Ryan, an elementary teacher and parent of two, said her next job is to be a face of hope for her classroom and the two children she and her husband share. “Everybody in the community has come together. I’ve never seen anything like this or experienced anything like this,” Ryan said. “Tomorrow, everybody’s going back to school, and as a fourth-grade teacher, I’m just going to try to make my kids’ lives feel as normal as possible.” Though she hasn’t convinced Cody to adopt any of the displaced animals, she said the couple did get a chance to paddle the Animas River at its record-breaking flow, just for fun. “I will tell you, best float of my life,” Ryan said.
